title: Share a contract

outcomes.can: Implement an interface and use the type through it.
Extend a class and override a method so the right version runs.
Write two types behind one interface and a method that works with both.

intro: Different types can often be used the same way: several places to read tasks from, several kinds of card. This module covers interfaces, which state what a type can do, and inheritance, where one type builds on another.

steps.title: An interface is a contract
steps.text: An interface lists members without bodies. interface ISource says that any source has a Name and a Count method. A class takes on the contract by naming the interface after a colon, as in class FixedSource : ISource, and must then provide every member. Having matching members is not enough: the class has to name the interface. A variable of type ISource can hold any object whose class implements it. Code written against ISource works with all of them, including classes written later.

steps.title: A class can build on another
steps.text: class UrgentNotice : Notice makes UrgentNotice a kind of Notice. It gets Title and Text from Notice (inheritance). : base(title) passes the title on to Notice's constructor. A method marked virtual in the base class may be replaced, and the derived class replaces it with override. Records can inherit the same way, for example record Arrived(int Count) : Update. A type marked abstract cannot be created itself. It exists only to be inherited from.

steps.title: Which Text runs?
steps.text: notice is declared as a Notice but holds an UrgentNotice. Predict the last line of output.

steps.title: Follow the calls
steps.text: The loop calls Name and Count through ISource and never needs to know the class. Each object answers with its own version. The same holds for notice.Text(). The variable's type is Notice, but the object is an UrgentNotice, and with virtual and override the object's own version runs, so the line is "Ship!". Without override, the derived method would only hide the base one, and a call through a Notice variable would run the base version.

steps.title: Leave out a member
steps.text: EmptySource names ISource but has no Count method. Read the example before checking.

steps.title: Read the compiler error
steps.text: Check the example. CS0535 says EmptySource does not implement the interface member ISource.Count(). The error is on the line that names the interface, because that is where the promise was made.

steps.title: Finish a task source
steps.text: The case box supplies the interface and a method that uses it. Finish the class so it keeps what it is given.

steps.title: Add an urgent card
steps.text: Work from the prompt. One check calls your method through a variable of the base type.

questions.prompt: What is the last line of output?

choices.feedback: Text is virtual and UrgentNotice overrides it, so the object's own version runs.
The object is an UrgentNotice. With virtual and override, its version runs whatever the variable's type is.
An UrgentNotice is a Notice, so the assignment is allowed.

questions.prompt: What happens when you check this example?

choices.feedback: The class promised ISource but has no Count. The compiler rejects that before running.

choices.text: It runs until Count is called, then stops.
choices.feedback: A missing interface member is found at compile time, not while running.

choices.text: The compiler reports an error on line 10.
choices.feedback: Line 10 names ISource, and the class does not provide Count (CS0535).

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter on a later visit, with the earlier answer closed. A first unaided pass on every case is later evidence of the skill. A hinted pass stays recorded as assisted.

drillGap: These drills practise one declaration each. They do not call a method through a base-type variable.
